title: AI Overviews Are Rewiring Search: What Changed in 2026
body_md:
![blog.google official page screenshot](https://afroditena.github.io/mattress-checklist-android/assets/img/ai-overviews-are-rewiring-search-what-changed-in-2026/1.png)
*Screenshot of blog.google ([source](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/sundar-pichai-io-2026/))*

Here's my bottom line: AI Overviews didn't kill search traffic in 2026 — they **repriced** it. Reading the published data, informational "how do I do X" content has lost a large share of its clicks when an AI Overview appears, and generic comparison content is hit nearly as hard (see Seer's 95.4% figure below). Content built on firsthand input — original testing, verified pricing — looks like the more defensible position. If you're still measuring your site's health by total organic sessions, you're tracking the wrong number and you're about to make some very bad decisions.

The less visible part is behavioral: Pew's browsing data shows people click traditional results less often when an AI summary appears, and online publishers have attributed declining web traffic to those summaries.

## What's Actually Going On

![pewresearch.org official page screenshot](https://afroditena.github.io/mattress-checklist-android/assets/img/ai-overviews-are-rewiring-search-what-changed-in-2026/2.png)
*Screenshot of pewresearch.org ([source](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2025/07/22/google-users-are-less-likely-to-click-on-links-when-an-ai-summary-appears-in-the-results/))*

### The scale is bigger than most people realize

This is no longer a niche feature. At Google I/O in May 2026, Sundar Pichai said AI Overviews had passed 2.5 billion monthly active users and AI Mode had surpassed 1 billion, one year after launch, with queries more than doubling every quarter since ([Google Search I/O 2026 post](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/search/search-io-2026)).

The structural change at the same event matters more than either number: Google merged AI Overviews and AI Mode into one integrated search experience worldwide, with Gemini 3.5 Flash as the default model. The summary is now the doorway into a conversation, not a box sitting above ten blue links.

### The click data is ugly, but it's ugly selectively

Pew's study is useful because it tracked real browsing rather than keyword-tool estimates. Analyzing 900 U.S. adults' browsing data, Pew found 58% of users ran at least one search that triggered an AI summary in March 2025; users clicked a traditional result link in 8% of visits to search pages with an AI summary versus 15% of visits without one — a 47% relative drop. Clicks on links inside the summaries happened in only 1% of visits, and users were more likely to abandon browsing after a page with a summary (26%) than without (16%).

Google disputed Pew's methodology, arguing the analysis period overlapped with unrelated algorithm testing.

Ahrefs, using a different method entirely, landed in the same direction. Its April 2025 comparison of forecasted vs. actual CTR suggested AI Overviews reduced position-1 click-through rate by about 34.5%. The February 2026 re-run, built on December 2025 data, measured position-1 CTR at 0.016 with an AI Overview present versus 0.039 without — a 58% reduction ([source](https://ahrefs.com/blog/ai-overviews-reduce-clicks-update/)). The damage thins down the page: position two down 50.8%, position ten down 19.4%. And 99.2% of keywords that trigger AI Overviews are informational in intent.

That last stat is the whole story, and almost nobody leads with it.

### The rebound is real — and it's a redistribution, not a recovery

Seer Interactive's longitudinal study is the most useful 2026 dataset I've seen. It covers 53 brands, 5.47 million queries, and 2.43 billion impressions, running January 2025 to February 2026.

Organic CTR on AIO-present queries climbed from a floor of 1.3% in December 2025 to 2.4% in February 2026 — an 85% jump in two months.

But look at the other side of the ledger: CTR on searches *without* AI Overviews rose from 2.8% in January 2025 to 3.8% by February 2026. One plausible reading (mine, not a measured finding) is that AI Overviews absorb the quick answers, so the users who still click are the ones who want more.

Cited pages outperform uncited pages on the same results page, but both still trail no-AIO searches. Seer itself calls this a levelling off rather than a recovery, and cautions against forecasting from two months of data.

And Seer's query-type breakdown contains the one finding that should reset a lot of assumptions: at a 95.4% AIO trigger rate, nearly every "X vs Y" informational query in their study had an AI Overview — meaning comparison-page traffic is almost certainly AIO-affected.

## The Counterpoint

![ahrefs.com official page screenshot](https://afroditena.github.io/mattress-checklist-android/assets/img/ai-overviews-are-rewiring-search-what-changed-in-2026/4.png)
*Screenshot of ahrefs.com ([source](https://ahrefs.com/blog/ai-overviews-reduce-clicks/))*

The strongest argument against me is that clicks were always a bad proxy for value, and the rebound proves the panic was overblown. Seer cautions that a CTR drop isn't automatically bad news: it found cited brands whose impressions more than doubled while clicks stayed flat, which pushed the ratio down. If AI Overviews strip out the low-intent drive-by visitors who were never going to convert, a site can lose 40% of its sessions and lose almost nothing that mattered. Fair. Some of the loudest traffic-collapse stories are businesses discovering their audience was never really theirs.

I still land where I started, for one reason: even *cited* pages get fewer clicks than pages on no-AIO searches. Being the source Google trusts most is still worse, click-wise, than the AI simply not showing up. That's not a quality filter. That's a structural discount on being on the web at all.

## Bottom Line

If you run a content site, a SaaS blog, or a personal brand that depends on search:

- **Stop reporting total organic sessions.** Split your reporting into AIO-present and AIO-absent queries. They're two different channels now with opposite trend lines.
- **Reconsider your explainer backlog.** In my view, content whose only job is to state a fact is a depreciating asset in 2026. Redirect that effort into things requiring firsthand input — tests, teardowns, pricing you verified, opinions with a name attached.
- **Treat citation as a real KPI**, but don't pretend it replaces traffic. Seer put cited pages at about 2.1% CTR versus 0.9% for uncited pages — roughly 2.3x, worth chasing, not worth betting the business on.
- **Build one channel Google can't intermediate.** Email, community, podcast, YouTube. Pick one and actually work it.

For searchers: open the underlying sources for prices, recent changes and judgment calls. Check dates and whether the source actually supports the answer. That's a practical verification habit, not a measured claim about AI Overview accuracy.

## FAQ

**Are AI Overviews reducing clicks for every kind of search?**
No. Ahrefs found 99.2% of AI Overview–triggering keywords are informational in intent, and Pew found only 8% of one- or two-word searches produced a summary versus 53% of searches with 10 or more words. Short, brand-specific queries are far less likely to trigger a summary than long conversational ones.

**Is the CTR decline reversing?**
Partially. Seer measured a floor of 1.3% in December 2025 rising to 2.4% by February 2026, but CTR on searches without AI Overviews rose to 3.8% over a comparable period, so the gap hasn't closed.

**Does getting cited in an AI Overview make up for lost traffic?**
It helps and it isn't enough. Pew found clicks on links inside AI summaries occurred in just 1% of visits. Citation is better than invisibility; it is not a traffic strategy on its own.

**Is AI Mode a bigger threat than AI Overviews?**
That framing expired in May 2026, when Google merged the two into one experience. AI Overviews still reach more people — 2.5 billion monthly users versus 1 billion for AI Mode — but AI Mode queries have been more than doubling every quarter, so the trajectory matters more than the current gap.

*Updated October 2026. This post is analysis of published studies (Ahrefs, Pew, Seer) and Google's own announcements, not original testing of my own. It was previously revised to update the Ahrefs figure to its February 2026 re-run (58%, up from 34.5% in April 2025), remove unsupported absolutes, and clarify that Pew's rates refer to visits to search pages. Sources: [Ahrefs](https://ahrefs.com/blog/ai-overviews-reduce-clicks-update/), [Pew Research Center](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2025/07/22/google-users-are-less-likely-to-click-on-links-when-an-ai-summary-appears-in-the-results/), [Seer Interactive](https://www.seerinteractive.com/insights/aio-impact-on-google-ctr-2026-update), [Google](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/sundar-pichai-io-2026/).*

## My Take

![seerinteractive.com official page screenshot](https://afroditena.github.io/mattress-checklist-android/assets/img/ai-overviews-are-rewiring-search-what-changed-in-2026/3.png)
*Screenshot of seerinteractive.com ([source](https://www.seerinteractive.com/insights/aio-impact-on-google-ctr-2026-update))*

The dominant narrative — "AI Overviews are destroying the open web" — is emotionally satisfying and strategically useless. My read is that Google automated the part of the web that was low-value: the 900-word article that exists solely to restate a fact you could have gotten in one sentence. The "how to convert PDF to Word" genre was never content; it was a toll booth built on top of an answer. Google removed the toll booth, and traffic fell. I don't think that's a tragedy.

The declines also aren't uniform, which is why averaging them is the real mistake. Pew found just 8% of one- or two-word searches produced an AI summary, rising to 53% for searches of 10 words or more. The long, conversational, explain-this-to-me query is AI Overview territory. The short, "I already know what I want" query largely isn't. Those are different businesses with different futures, and one "organic traffic" line hides that completely.

Here's where I'll get specific, because the data pushes somewhere uncomfortable: **the comparison-content safe harbor is closing.** For most of 2025 the advice was "pivot to comparison and buying-intent content, AI Overviews don't touch it." Seer's 95.4% AIO rate on "X vs Y" queries says that window is basically shut for generic comparisons. What survives isn't the *format*, it's the *input* — original testing, real pricing someone actually paid, screenshots, judgment a model can't synthesize from three other summaries. An AI Overview can compress consensus. It can't manufacture a firsthand call that doesn't exist on the web yet.

To the reader who says this is just SEOs whining about a platform change: partly, yes, and the rebound data gives that argument teeth — if your clicks were low-intent, losing them cost you less than your dashboard suggests. But the second-order effect is real. Pew found Reddit, Wikipedia and YouTube among the most-cited sources in AI summaries, and when synthesis pays and origination doesn't, you get more synthesis and fewer people doing the original work synthesis depends on. That's a slow problem, not a loud one, which is exactly why it's easy to ignore.

If you take one thing into your next planning cycle, make it this: stop forecasting off a blended CTR, and assume that anything you publish whose only asset is a restated fact will be worth less in twelve months than it is today.
